subject: english-literature
title: Heathcliff, the Byronic Hero and the Gothic Double
welcome_lead: Analyse Heathcliff as Byronic hero, racial outsider, and Gothic double — and trace the novel's preoccupation with merged identity.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on Heathcliff in Wuthering Heights: Byronic hero, racial outsider, and the Catherine double.
final_note: Catherine says 'I am Heathcliff'. The novel takes the claim literally and tracks what happens to two people who refuse to be two.

concepts.def: Romantic protagonist after Byron's Childe Harold and Manfred: brooding, transgressive, mysterious origin, alienated from social norms.
Brought from Liverpool by old Mr Earnshaw; his racial identity is ambiguous (called 'dark', 'gipsy', 'Lascar'); critics debate the novel's relation to the Atlantic slave trade.
Catherine's 'I am Heathcliff' (Ch. 9) declares fused identity; the novel literalises Gothic doubling beyond metaphor.
After Catherine's marriage to Edgar, Heathcliff returns mysteriously wealthy and methodically destroys both families through marriage and inheritance.
Brontë's Gothic fuses Radcliffean atmosphere with German Romanticism (Hoffmann); the supernatural is sustained but never settled.
Critics including Susan Meyer and Elsie Michie read Heathcliff's racial coding as central; the novel registers Britain's imperial guilt obliquely.

walkthroughs.body_html: Heathcliff inherits the Byronic hero from Childe Harold (1812-18) and Manfred (1817): outsider origin, hyperbolic passion, indifference to social code, sublime rage. Brontë knew Byron through her brother Branwell. But Heathcliff differs: he is not aristocratic, his vengeance is patient and economic, and his interiority is largely closed to the reader. Critics like Stevie Davies argue Brontë transforms the type by removing aristocratic glamour.

Old Earnshaw finds Heathcliff on the streets of Liverpool in 1771. Liverpool was then Britain's primary slave-trading port. Critics including Susan Meyer ('Reading Wuthering Heights') and Maja-Lisa von Sneidern have argued Heathcliff may be coded as a child of mixed race or from the African diaspora. The novel's racial language — 'dark', 'gipsy', 'imp of Satan' — registers Atlantic anxieties without ever resolving them. AO5 responses gain from acknowledging this critical opening.

Catherine's Chapter 9 confession to Nelly — 'Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same' / 'I am Heathcliff' — pushes Romantic identification past metaphor. Critics including Patricia Yaeger and Stevie Davies read this as a Gothic literalisation of doubled selfhood. Catherine's later illness and Heathcliff's posthumous wandering enact the failure of separation. The grave-digging scene (Ch. 29) makes the doubling physical.
